name: Bilal Alvarez

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me, Bilal. I'm a researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no connection to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say is confidential. What does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run an electric rope shovel at a large copper mine, the biggest digging machine on site. It's like a four-storey building with a bucket the size of a garage, and I load the haul trucks, three or four passes each. Shifts are twelve hours, and for the last few months two of my days each swing have been in the remote trial, running the shovel's assist system from a chair in the operations centre.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like, and what wears on you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the numbers, honestly. The shovel logs every dig, so I can see my cycle time, payload, how long the trucks wait on me, and I paste my weekly stats into an AI chat to find where I'm losing seconds. What wears on me is the commute, ninety minutes each way on the bus, and the noise. Even with earmuffs, you feel the hoist in your chest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the one we call AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Interesting. I don't think that's where it's going, but okay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, fair enough, it's a tool and not a miracle, and I'd keep using it. Most of the guys would be pleased, so I wouldn't rub it in. Online I'd probably not say much, I mostly lurk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, it'd mean I keep doing what I'm doing and the remote trial becomes normal over time. I'd probably end up as one of the people who runs the shovels from the operations centre. Not a huge change, just a slightly better job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going with my online certificate in mine production planning, which I'm doing at night. I'd keep putting a few hundred a month into an index fund, on top of about four months of cash savings. And I'd keep pushing for more days in the remote trial.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Maybe a little bored.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does a production planner actually do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They work out where the shovels dig, in what order, so the right rock goes to the crusher and the trucks don't bunch up. Right now they use software for most of it. I like it because it's the brain of the operation.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you wouldn't rub it in. Who would you be careful around?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frank, who trained me on the shovel, thinks the remote trial is a waste of money. He's fifty-eight and a brilliant operator. I'd let him have his win, he's earned it.

S0.say: I'd say fair enough, it's a tool and not a miracle, and I'd keep using it. I wouldn't rub it in at work, since most colleagues would be pleased.
S0.think: I think I'd keep doing what I do while the remote trial becomes normal, probably ending up running shovels from the operations centre. It'd be a slightly better job, not a huge change.
S0.do: Continues his night-time online certificate in mine production planning and keeps putting a few hundred a month into an index fund on top of about four months of cash. Pushes for more days in the remote trial.
S0.quote: I'd let him have his win, he's earned it.
S0.fieldNote: He's already deep in data and remote operation, so the plateau barely registers. He's careful not to gloat, showing respect for older operators like his trainer. His savings and investing habits are already in place.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yeah. That one I'd bet on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's happening, so the smart thing is to learn the new systems instead of fighting them. I'd also say the company should give everyone a fair shot at training, not just the young ones. I'd say that in the crib room, and probably to my supervisor.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think it's good for me, honestly. I'm already on the remote trial and I'm learning planning. The risk is that there are fewer seats in the operations centre than there are operators.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask to be in the remote trial full-time and finish the planning certificate this year. I'd apply for a junior planner role the first time one comes up. I'd keep investing, maybe a bit more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Focused, maybe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned fewer seats than operators. How do you feel about getting one ahead of others?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mixed. I'd take it, I'm not going to pretend I wouldn't. But I'd also try to help the guys who want to learn, like I showed two of them how to read the dig logs last month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if the planner role didn't come up?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd look at other mines. There's a gold operation about two hours away that's hiring for remote operations. I'd move for the right job.

S1.say: I'd say it's happening, so the smart move is to learn the new systems rather than fight them. I'd also say the company should give everyone a fair chance at training, not just young workers.
S1.think: I think it's good for me, since I'm already in the remote trial and learning planning. The risk is that there are fewer seats in the operations centre than there are operators.
S1.do: Asks to join the remote trial full-time and finishes the planning certificate this year. Applies for the first junior planner role that comes up, invests a bit more, and looks at remote jobs at another mine if needed.
S1.quote: I'd take it, I'm not going to pretend I wouldn't.
S1.fieldNote: He expects to come out ahead and was frank about taking a scarce seat over others. He helps colleagues learn the dig logs, which softens that. He'd move for the right job, unlike more rooted colleagues.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Next one, AGI by 2028. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. Okay, that's a different game.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's going to be rough and that the government should have a plan for people who lose their jobs, because there'll be a lot of us. But I wouldn't be marching. I'd be the guy saying, okay, what's the move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think it hits me later than most, but it does hit me. If AI can do almost any job, it can plan a mine and run a shovel. My edge is that I'd be one of the people who sets it up, and then it doesn't need me either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd try to get onto the team that installs the new systems, because that's where the work is in the first year. I'd push my cash savings from four months to eight, and stop adding to the index fund while I do. I'd also sell my second motorbike, which I don't need.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Interested and worried at the same time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said it doesn't need you either, after setup. What then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know, and that's the bit that bugs me. Maybe I'd own some shares in the companies doing the replacing. I'd hope the government does something like a basic income, but I wouldn't count on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does two years of warning actually buy someone like you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A front-row seat, mainly. I'd see what's coming before most people at the mine and could jump on the right team. But two years is not enough to build something new that lasts.

S2.say: I'd say it'll be rough and the government should have a plan for the many people who lose jobs. I wouldn't be marching, I'd be asking what the move is.
S2.think: I think it hits me later than most but still hits me, since AI could plan a mine and run a shovel. My edge is setting it up, and then it doesn't need me either.
S2.do: Tries to join the team installing the new systems in the first year. Pushes cash savings from four to eight months, pauses index fund contributions and sells his second motorbike.
S2.feel: Anxious, with interest and worry at the same time.
S2.quote: My edge is that I'd be one of the people who sets it up, and then it doesn't need me either.
S2.fieldNote: Even an adaptive, data-minded operator sees only a temporary role in the fast scenario. He shifts money from investing to cash, a sign he's taking it seriously. He's sceptical that government help would come.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now AGI by 2031. The same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's still fast, but more time to play.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a serious change, and it's on all of us to get ready, workers, companies and government. I'd tell the younger guys to learn the systems now. And I'd say anyone over fifty needs proper support.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'd do fine for most of those five years and then need a plan B. The planner job might be gone by 2031 too. So I'd want something on the side that's mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the planning certificate and move into a planner role within a year or two. On the side, I'd start a small business fixing and selling e-bikes and motorbikes, using AI to handle the listings and paperwork. And I'd keep investing, since if machines do the work, owning part of them makes sense.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Fine day to day, but I'd be watching.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why bikes, of all things?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's my hobby already. I've got a mate, Tomás, who's a mechanic, and we've done up four bikes in his garage this year and sold three. People will still want someone they trust to look at their bike, at least for a while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Isn't a bike repair business also something robots could do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sure, eventually. But it's small and it's local, and I'd own it. I'd rather own a small thing that gets hit late than work for a big thing that gets hit early.

S3.say: I'd say it's a serious change and workers, companies and government all need to get ready. I'd tell younger workers to learn the systems now and say people over fifty need proper support.
S3.think: I think I'd do fine for most of those five years but would need a plan B, since even planning might be automated by 2031. I'd want something on the side that's mine.
S3.do: Finishes the planning certificate and moves into a planner role within a year or two. Starts a small side business fixing and selling bikes with a mechanic friend, using AI for listings and paperwork, and keeps investing.
S3.feel: Uneasy, fine day to day but watchful.
S3.quote: I'd rather own a small thing that gets hit late than work for a big thing that gets hit early.
S3.fieldNote: With five years he builds a second leg, a small bike business, and explains it with a clear ownership logic. His centre outlook shows in sharing responsibility between workers, companies and government. He still believes in investing as a hedge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Last one, AGI by 2036. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. Yeah, I like my odds there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough for a smooth transition if people actually use it. I'd tell everyone at work to start a plan now. I'd probably post about it too, the practical stuff, which courses, which jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think ten years works well for me. By thirty-seven I'd have planning experience, a small business and some investments. The risk is mostly for the people who don't move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd move into planning within two years, then try for a role managing the automated fleet. I'd grow the bike business slowly and keep investing every month. I'd probably buy a small unit closer to the mine, to cut the ninety-minute commute.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Optimistic, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Frank in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him he's got enough time to retire on his own terms, which is the best news he could get. And I'd ask him to teach me everything about how the shovel behaves in bad ground, because that knowledge has to go into the system somehow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that would still worry you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That I'm wrong about it being a smooth ten years. If it's slow and then sudden, the last two years could look like the 2028 picture. So I'd keep that eight months of cash, just in case.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is enough for a smooth transition if people use it. I'd tell colleagues to start planning now and post practical tips about courses and jobs.
S4.think: I think ten years works well for me, since by 37 I'd have planning experience, a small business and investments. The risk is mostly for people who don't move.
S4.do: Moves into planning within two years and then aims to manage the automated fleet. Grows the bike business, keeps investing monthly and buys a small unit closer to the mine to cut his commute.
S4.quote: If it's slow and then sudden, the last two years could look like the 2028 picture.
S4.fieldNote: The long timeline suits him and he's openly optimistic. He sees value in older operators' knowledge and wants to capture it. He still keeps a cash buffer in case the change speeds up at the end.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. What would help is honest information early, like the company telling us its automation plans, plus short, cheap courses in the new systems. And some kind of safety net from the government, though I'm not sure what shape it should take.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: What the old operators know. Frank can hear when the ground's going bad from the sound of the bucket. If nobody writes that down before he retires, the robots will have to learn it the hard way.

headlineQuote: Frank can hear when the ground's going bad from the sound of the bucket.
portrait: Bilal is a 27-year-old electric rope shovel operator at a large copper mine with about four months of cash savings and a small index fund. He's curious and data-minded, uses AI tools all the time, including to study his dig stats, is in the mine's remote operations trial and is studying production planning at night. He's calm in the plateau and steady change, expecting to come out ahead, though he's frank about taking scarce seats. AGI in two years makes him anxious, since he sees only a short setup role, while five and ten years let him build a planning career, a bike business with a friend and steady investments. He values the know-how of older operators like his trainer Frank.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, because there'd only be a short window of setup work before he wasn't needed.
whatWouldHelp: Honest early information on company automation plans, short affordable courses in the new systems, and some form of government safety net.
